query: For a high-entropy alloy coating system on a transition metal matrix, what is the relationship between ambient temperature and tribological performance? Please hypothesize the dominant mechanism linking thermal conditions to wear resistance and propose a boundary where performance degrades.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings on transition metal matrices, tribological performance exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with ambient temperature: wear resistance initially improves with rising temperature due to the formation of a protective tribo-oxide layer, but degrades significantly beyond a critical threshold where tribochemical reactions become excessive, leading to high friction coefficients and accelerated wear.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) coating (e.g., CuMoTaWV or AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5) deposited on a transition metal matrix (e.g., 304 stainless steel or MoNbTaTiW), characterized by a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution structure with grain sizes ~18 nm and high hardness (~19 GPa).
generation.intervention: Exposure to elevated ambient temperatures (from room temperature up to 300°C and beyond) during sliding wear tests against a steel counterface under constant load (1 N) and sliding distance.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric environment (air), sliding contact with alloy steel counterball, constant normal load (1 N), varying temperatures (RT to >300°C).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and evolution of a tribo-oxide layer (e.g., CuO, Cr2O3, or mixed oxides) on the wear track surface, which acts as a solid lubricant at moderate temperatures but becomes unstable and thick at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At moderate temperatures (RT to ~200°C), the HEA coating maintains high hardness and forms a thin, protective oxide layer that reduces friction and wear. As temperature increases beyond ~250-300°C, tribochemical reactions accelerate, leading to excessive oxide formation, increased coefficient of friction (COF), and loss of protective layer integrity, causing a sharp increase in wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Wear resistance will improve slightly from RT to ~200°C due to oxide layer formation, but will degrade significantly above 250-300°C, with wear rates increasing by 1-2 orders of magnitude and COF rising from ~0.25 to >1.0.
generation.baseline: Room temperature wear behavior of as-deposited or annealed HEA coatings, showing moderate wear rates (~6.4×10⁻⁶ mm³/N·m) and low COF (~0.25).
generation.boundary: Performance degradation threshold: 250-300°C, beyond which tribochemical reactions dominate and protective oxide layers become unstable, leading to catastrophic wear increase.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold temperature may vary depending on specific HEA composition, coating microstructure, and environmental conditions (e.g., humidity, oxygen partial pressure). The mechanism may differ for different HEA systems (e.g., FCC vs. BCC structures).
generation.falsification_experiment: Conduct wear tests on the same HEA coating system at temperatures ranging from RT to 400°C in controlled atmospheres (air, argon, vacuum) to isolate the role of tribochemical reactions. Measure wear rates, COF, and oxide layer composition at each temperature. If wear resistance continues to improve or remains stable above 300°C without degradation, the hypothesis is falsified.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
